generated_answer:
Positional encoding in the Transformer is a mechanism used to inject information about the relative or absolute position of tokens in a sequence into the model. This is necessary because the Transformer architecture, which relies on self-attention mechanisms, does not have recurrence or convolution, and therefore cannot inherently capture the order of the sequence.

The positional encoding used in the Transformer is based on sine and cosine functions of different frequencies, as described in the following equations:

_PE_ ( _pos,_ 2 _i_ ) = _sin_ ( _pos/_ 10000 [2] _[i/d]_ [model] )

_PE_ ( _pos,_ 2 _i_ +1) = _cos_ ( _pos/_ 10000 [2] _[i/d]_ [model] )

where _pos_ is the position and _i_ is the dimension. This allows the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset _k_, _PEpos_ + _k_ can be represented as a linear function of _PEpos_ [Vaswani et al. 2017, pp.6].

The use of positional encoding is necessary because the self-attention mechanism in the Transformer does not have a notion of position, and therefore cannot capture the order of the sequence. By adding positional encoding to the input embeddings, the model can learn to attend to different positions in the sequence, which is essential for tasks such as machine translation [Vaswani et al. 2017, pp.6].

A pooling layer is a type of layer in a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) that aims to gradually reduce the dimensionality of the representation, and thus further reduce the number of parameters and the computational complexity of the model [O'Shea and Nash 2015, pp.8].

The pooling layer operates over each activation map in the input, and scales its dimensionality using the "MAX" function. In most CNNs, these come in the form of max-pooling layers with kernels of a dimensionality of 2 × 2 applied with a stride of 2 along the spatial dimensions of the input [O'Shea and Nash 2015, pp.8].

The role of the pooling layer is to perform downsampling along the spatial dimensionality of the given input, further reducing the number of parameters within that activation [O'Shea and Nash 2015, pp.9]. This helps to reduce the complexity of the model and prevent overfitting.
